briefs.headline: Asian Games-bound athletes set for one final test
briefs.bodyText:
The focus will squarely be on the big names travelling for the Asian Games as the invitation-only, season-ending Indian Athletics Final Series at the Jawaharlal Nehru Stadium here on Thursday is set to be the most decorated domestic event of the calendar year.
The Athletics Federation of India has opted for 30 disciplines — 15 each in men and women — in the one-day, single-session event. The cream of Indian track and field, including almost all the Asiad-bound names, will be looking to assess their competition worthiness one last time ahead of the continental extravaganza.
The athletes were invited as per their ranking across the Athletics Series through the year, with the quartermilers expected to be in the spotlight. In men’s 400m, National record holder Vishal T.K., Rajesh Ramesh, Manu T.S., Dharamveer Chaudhary, Mohammed Ashfaq and Jay Kumar have all been called up to compete.
Vishal has also been named in the 200m start list along with Animesh Kujur, who will also be gunning to regain his title of the fastest Indian man in 100m.
NR holder Gurindervir Singh and Harjit Singh are in the shortest sprint, the former hoping to allay fitness concerns. Also returning to action after almost a year and half out with injury and rehab is Avinash Sable in 3000m steeplechase. Ten of the 15 Asian Games medallists from Hangzhou who are bound for Aichi-Nagoya have been named in the start list.
There is no 200m for women while men’s discus throw hasn’t been included either. Harita Bhadra, a late addition to the Asiad squad after winning the 200m National Inter-State championships title in June with a season’s best effort, will be running in 100m along with Unnathi Bollanda Aiyappa.
Yashvir Singh, having made the cut after Neeraj Chopra was ruled out with injury, and Rohit Yadav, will both start in men’s javelin throw while Annu Rani will do so in the women’s section. Shot putter Tajinderpal Singh Toor will also compete for honours.
Some of the athletes have been given exemption, including Murali Sreeshankar (long jump), Praveen Chithravel (triple jump) and Sarvesh Kushare (high jump). The more gruelling events like middle and long-distance runs and decathlon have not been included.

briefs.headline: 'I don’t see who else can fight for the belt': Fiorot stakes UFC title claim
briefs.deck: Manon Fiorot believes a win over Alexa Grasso at Noche UFC will strengthen her case for a title shot in the women’s flyweight division. With Valentina Shevchenko vacating the belt due to injury, Fiorot sees an opportunity to fight for the title more quickly. The No. 2 contender says she has beaten all the contenders in the division and insists: “I don’t see who else can fight for the belt
briefs.bodyText:
Manon Fiorot has already decided what a win over Alexa Grasso should lead to.
“I think the winner of this fight will be the next one for the belt,” Fiorot told TimesofIndia.com ahead of her flyweight bout against Grasso at UFC Noche on September 13 at Glendale, Arizona. “I'm pretty sure the winner on Saturday evening will fight for the belt in the next fight.”
The title picture had changed just days before Fiorot's fight. On September 5, the UFC announced that Valentina Shevchenko had vacated the women's flyweight championship after telling the promotion she would be unable to compete for at least a year.
Shevchenko had been scheduled to defend the belt against No. 1 contender Natalia Silva at UFC 332 on October 3, but her injury forced that fight to be scrapped. Shevchenko is expected to return and compete for the title once she is healthy.
The vacant belt will now be contested by Silva and Wang Cong in the UFC 332 main event in Salt Lake City. Silva is 8-0 in the UFC and has won 14 straight fights, with her recent run including victories over former champions Rose Namajunas and Grasso, as well as former title challenger Jessica Andrade.
Shevchenko’s exit changes the title picture
For Fiorot, ranked No. 2, the change has made the route to another title opportunity look shorter.
The 36-year-old French fighter is 13-2 as a professional and 8-1 in the UFC. Her only UFC defeat came against Shevchenko in a five-round decision at UFC 315 in May 2025, after Fiorot had opened her UFC career with seven straight wins. She returned five months later and stopped Jasmine Jasudavicius in 1:14 of the first round.
Fiorot has also beaten Namajunas and former title challenger Erin Blanchfield during her UFC run.
“Yes, I think it's better for me,” Fiorot said of Shevchenko's departure. “Because it will allow the whole category to fight more. And I think I will have the title fight more quickly than if it was Valentina. I would have had to wait for Valentina if she had won in October.”
The immediate hurdle though is Grasso, the No. 3 contender and former UFC women's flyweight champion.
The 33-year-old Mexican enters with a 17-5-1 professional record. She became champion in March 2023 after submitting Shevchenko with a fourth-round face crank. Their rematch six months later ended in a split draw before Shevchenko regained the belt with a unanimous decision in their third meeting in September 2024.
Grasso then lost a unanimous decision to Silva at UFC 315. She returned in March this year with a first-round stoppage of Maycee Barber, putting herself back among the division's leading contenders.
And that bout piqued Fiorot’s interest.
“In the top five, she is the only girl I haven't fought again,” Fiorot said. “So after her great performance against Maycee, I think it's time. It's a good opportunity for us to fight together.”
Fiorot sees no one ahead of her
Fiorot's own case for another title opportunity rests on the opponents she has already beaten. Asked what argument she would make for being next rather than the winner of the Silva-Wang title fight, she was direct.
“Because I have beaten all the contenders in the division. So I don't see who else can fight for the belt.”
For now, though, Fiorot is resisting the temptation to look beyond Grasso.
“To be honest, I try not to think about it too much,” she said. “For now, I'm really focused on the fight with Alexa.”
“Yes, that's what [title shot] I want and what I would like, but I try not to think about it too much. For now, I'm focused on Saturday. And after, we have time to dream about it and focus on it. This is my goal. But right now, I'm thinking about Alexa and that's it.”
Fiorot has had almost 11 months to prepare since her last fight. The Jasudavicius stoppage lasted only 1:14, leaving little time to see the changes she had been working on during that period.
“I worked on a lot of things, but I won't say everything now,” Fiorot said. “But I hope I can show you a bit more against Grasso. I worked on a lot of skills and things, but, to be honest, I can't talk about them in the interview because of the game plan and the strategy. But I hope to show more and to show all my skills Saturday evening.”
The long gap between fights, she said, gave her time to work on areas that might not receive the same attention during a conventional fight camp.
“Yes, it allowed me to improve on a lot of things,” Fiorot said. “Because when you train for a fight, you train specifically for a fight. So I was able to work on a lot of things during all those months.”
“And yes, I think I'm even better today. Definitely, I think I'm a much better fighter now than 11 months ago.”
A French MMA wave closing in on UFC gold
Fiorot is also part of a strong group of French fighters pushing toward the top of the UFC. Ciryl Gane is the promotion's interim heavyweight champion and No. 1 heavyweight, Nassourdine Imavov is ranked No. 3 at middleweight, while Benoît Saint Denis is No. 
6 at lightweight.
Asked whether younger French fighters now see her as a reference point, Fiorot was unequivocal.
“Yes, clearly. The French fighters are clearly rising. We are very close to the belt.”
“So yes, I think it's good for the French MMA scene and for all the young people who are coming. Definitely, I think the hype of French MMA is big and it's a good thing for every fighter, every French fighter.”
Watch NOCHE UFC - Rodriguez vs Silva on September 13, 2026, from 2:30 AM IST live on Sony Sports Ten 2 SD & HD, Sony Sports Ten 3 SD & HD (Hindi), Sony Sports Ten 4 SD (Tamil, Telugu, Kannada) & Sony LIV.

briefs.headline: Duleep Trophy final | Individual milestones don’t matter as much as the result: Tilak
briefs.deck: The South Zone skipper stands tall in the summit clash with a valiant 99 against East Zone
briefs.bodyText:
Skipper Tilak Varma has been the standout player for South Zone in the Duleep Trophy this year.
The Hyderabad batter was instrumental in taking the team to the final, leading from the front with unbeaten knocks of 116 and 51 in the semifinal against North.
In the summit clash, Tilak yet again stood tall, scoring a valiant 99 against East Zone, even if he couldn’t help his team avoid conceding a huge lead.
“It’s an important knock, but at the same time I was only focused on what the team needed. I could have taken more chances before, but the plan was simply to take it session by session,” said Tilak.
“If some other batter stayed with me, I was confident we [could] have batted through to the end of the day, [and] take it session-by-session till tomorrow and push for a draw. Unfortunately, we lost wickets, and the result went in their favour,” he added.
“A hundred would have been a nice reward for the hard yards I put in the heat, but individual milestones don’t matter as much as the result.”
Though the 23-year-old has quickly been elevated as vice-captain of the T20I side, he reiterated that Test cricket is his ultimate goal.
“I always say to everyone that I want to play red-ball cricket for India. That’s my biggest goal because I really love playing red-ball cricket. As a kid, I thought I’d play Test cricket first and then only white-ball cricket. I’m really keen to play red-ball cricket, and let’s see how it goes,” said Tilak.

briefs.headline: Sheetal wins two medals, India finishes second in medal’s table
briefs.bodyText:
Armless para-archer Sheetal Devi won two medals, including a gold, as India secured six medals on the concluding day of the World Archery Para Series on Tuesday. The host finished second with its tally of four gold, three silver and eight bronze, behind Czechia, which topped the table with five gold.
Sheetal combined with Toman Kumar to get past Iraq’s Hameed Sarah and Kadhim Abbas 157-145 for the compound mixed team bronze. Then, she pipped Kazakhstan’s Seidan Aizada 144-144 (shoot-off 10-9) in the final to bag the women’s individual gold.
In the recurve mixed team final, Bhawna and Harvinder Singh defeated China’s Lang Quirong and Xia Lei 6-0 to claim the day’s second gold. Later, Bhawna outsmarted compatriot Rajshri Rathod 6-0 for the women’s individual bronze.

briefs.headline: 'That was some tennis!': Sachin Tendulkar in awe of Shelton’s epic win over Alcaraz
briefs.deck: Ben Shelton triumphed over Carlos Alcaraz in a thrilling five-set clash during the US Open quarter-finals. After an exhausting battle that stretched over four hours, Shelton emerged victorious, ending Alcaraz's impressive Grand Slam winning streak and title defense. Notably, this victory marked Shelton's first against a top-three ranked player, proving his prowess on the court, especially as…
briefs.bodyText:
Indian cricket legend 
Sachin Tendulkar
 was left impressed by the intensity of the Ben Shelton-Carlos Alcaraz battle at the US Open, describing their quarter-final clash as “some tennis” after a gripping five-set contest that went down to the final few points.
Shelton stunned defending champion Alcaraz 6-7(5), 6-1, 6-3, 1-6, 7-6(10-7) in a dramatic encounter that lasted four hours and 28 minutes. The American held his nerve in the deciding tiebreak to pull off one of the biggest wins of his career.
Taking to X, Tendulkar praised the fighting spirit shown by both players throughout the marathon contest.
“That was some tennis! Every time it looked like one of them had the match, the other fought his way back. And then it came down to the final few points.
Well played, Ben Shelton! Tough luck, Carlos. Coming back after an injury makes this one even tougher,” Tendulkar wrote.
A battle that refused to settle
Tendulkar's assessment captured the nature of a match that swung repeatedly between Shelton and Alcaraz.
Alcaraz took the opening set in a tiebreak, but Shelton responded emphatically, winning the next two sets to move within one of a place in the semi-finals. 
The Spaniard, however, refused to go quietly, taking the fourth set 6-1 and forcing a decider.
The fifth set ultimately needed a 10-point tiebreak, with Shelton prevailing 10-7. He then finished the job in emphatic fashion, firing a 146 mph ace on match point. The contest also became the latest-finishing match in US Open history, ending at 3:33 a.m. in New York.
Shelton ends Alcaraz's title defence
The victory ended Alcaraz's 18-match Grand Slam winning streak and sent Shelton into the US Open semi-finals, where he will face fellow American Frances Tiafoe. It was also Shelton's first career victory over a top-three opponent.
For Alcaraz, the defeat came during his first tournament since a four-and-a-half-month layoff because of a right wrist injury. Despite the loss, the Spaniard said he was proud of how he fought back during the contest.

briefs.headline: Duleep Trophy final | East does not give South an inch, coronation all but a matter of time
briefs.deck: Despite a 372-run lead, Kishan opts to bat the opposition out of the game and, at stumps, East reaches 212 for five in its second innings, ahead by 584 runs
briefs.bodyText:
A five-day First Class match in India — usually reserved for knockout fixtures — is designed to give teams a chance to push for an outright result.
At the same time, it tends to produce oddities because the focus is on securing the first-innings lead, which is enough to claim victory. Once that is achieved, the contest often fizzles out. Yet the teams still have to go through the motions until at least Tea on the final day, even if the outcome is a foregone conclusion.
The 2026 Duleep Trophy final between South Zone and East Zone in all likelihood will go down in history as one such game after the latter secured the crucial first-innings lead on the fourth day at the MAC Stadium here.
South, resuming at 242 for six in pursuit of East’s massive 708, was bundled out for 336 at lunch on Wednesday.
Realistically, South’s best hope was to delay the inevitable, and that relied on Tilak Varma getting a big one. For the first two hours of the penultimate day, the left-hander did just that, positively countering Mohammed Shami and Mukesh Kumar’s burst with the second new ball.
C.V. Milind supported his captain, with the duo adding 78 for the seventh wicket. But once Shikhar Mohan had Milind caught at short-leg, the end was near.
Tilak, in a rush to get to his landmark, fell agonisingly short by one run while trying to push for a single, only to give a simple return catch to off-spinner Kounain Quraishi.
Despite a 372-run lead, Ishan Kishan opted to bat the opposition out of the game and, at stumps, East was 212 for five in its second innings, ahead by 584 runs.
Though the contest was virtually sealed, a healthy crowd had gathered in the hope of seeing Vaibhav Sooryavanshi put on a show. The southpaw, though, perished early, stumped while attempting to charge down off-spinner T. Vijay.
Kishan — who smashed 270 in the first essay — continued from where he left off, stroking his way to a flamboyant 80 (98b, 9x4, 3x6). He was severe on spinners Vijay and Shreyas Gopal, repeatedly stepping down at every opportunity and carting them all over the park to entertain the fans.
